title: The tiger raised by goats
hookLine: a tiger who thinks he's a goat sees his face in the water
carry: see the seer, and the ego winds down
tomorrow: The boy who asked for nothing
last: THE MIND IS SEEN; THE SELF IS THE LIGHT.

lines: LOOK AT YOUR FACE IN THE WATER.
cards: Sri Ramakrishna, the nineteenth-century saint of Bengal, liked to tell this one. A tigress dies giving birth beside a flock of goats, and the cub grows up among them. He eats grass.
He bleats. He's sure he's a goat. One day a wild tiger comes, and the grass-eater bleats in terror with the rest.
The old tiger catches him and drags him to a pond. Look at your face in the water, he says. It's just like mine.
The cub bleats a few more times. Then, slowly, he roars.

teach.b: Ramakrishna told it about the teacher who shows you what you already are. Patanjali names the same turning point in sutra 4.25: visheshadarshina atmabhava-bhavana-vinivrittih.
For the one who sees the distinction, the making of a self comes to an end. The distinction is yesterday's: the mind is seen, the seer sees.
Atmabhava-bhavana is the habit of building a self out of the mind's material, rehearsing it, feeding it. The cub did that every day: I'm the one who eats grass, I'm the one who bleats.
Hindu thought has a plain name for that self-building: the ego.
Samkhya calls it ahamkara, the I-maker; Patanjali calls the feeling asmita, taking the instrument of seeing for the seer. One look in the water, and the bleating loses its point.
Then the mind slopes toward discernment and leans toward freedom.

teach.h: SEE THE SEER, AND THE EGO WINDS DOWN.
teach.b: Nimna means low ground, the slope water runs down. Freedom stops being a climb. It's downhill.
Patanjali stays honest, though. The very next sutra admits that old impressions still throw up other thoughts. The cub bleated a few more times before he roared.
We build selves too: out of grades, followers, being the funny one or the smart one, and we keep rehearsing them. Hindu teaching doesn't ask you to fight that self to the death.
It asks you to see what you are, and let the act get quieter.

how: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras describe viveka, discernment between the seer and the seen, as the turning point of the path; after it, practice is said to become less a struggle and more a natural leaning toward freedom.

o: a humble bow, the head lowered before a teacher
a low mood that pulls the mind down into sadness
low, sloping ground, where the mind runs to freedom

games.q: the cub and the sutra — tap the pairs.
p: the habit of making a self

s: in 4.26 the mind slopes toward discernment
viveka-nimnam: tilted like ground that water runs down.
after 4.25, old impressions never surface again
4.27 admits that in the gaps, old impressions still throw up other thoughts. the cub bleated a few more times.
the end of the sense of I comes from a clever answer
it comes from seeing, like the cub seeing his own face in the water.

games.q: the cub has seen his face in the pond. what do sutras 4.25–4.27 say comes next?
o: he must fight the goat in himself every day, forever.
the self-making habit winds down and the mind slopes toward freedom, though old bleats still surface.
he never bleats again, not even once.
games.why: seeing the distinction ends the self-making habit; the mind tilts toward freedom; old impressions still surface in the gaps (4.27).

practice: Sit tall, then let your weight settle into the seat, the way water settles into low ground. As small I-thoughts come by, I should, I'm tired, I wonder, let each one roll downhill and away.
Rest in whatever is left when they've passed.

wordCard.voice: Nimna, low, sloping ground. Seeing the seer and the seen as different, the habit of building a self out of the mind winds down, and the mind slopes toward freedom.

orig.note: Sanskrit nimna: low, sloping ground. in 4.26 the mind slopes toward discernment.

carryVoice: Your line: see the seer, and the ego winds down. One look in the water, and the bleating stopped. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna (the tiger cub raised among goats, shown its face in the water)
Yoga Sutra 4.25, Vyasa's commentary (the self-questions that cease)
Yoga Sutra 4.27 (old impressions in the gaps)
Yoga Sutra 2.6 (asmita: the seer and the instrument of seeing taken as one)
